Q-04.reply:
i usually spend weeks researching before making any big non-essential purchase, even something like a bike or a piece of furniture that i can live without if needed. 

for example, with the used car last year... i looked at 20 different listings over a month, read every review on multiple sites, and test drove three cars before settling on one. 

the key is to just stop looking once you've found something that checks all your boxes. overthinking it can lead to analysis paralysis and you end up not buying anything.

i also tend to lean towards boring, reliable options that won't need frequent repairs or replacements down the line. a 10-year old car that still runs well, for instance, is preferable to a flashy new one with a long payment plan.

and of course, i always prioritize cash over debt. if something's only available on finance, it's not worth the stress and extra cost in my mind.

so to summarize... lots of research up front, a focus on reliability over flashiness, and avoiding debt whenever possible are my usual strategies for making big non-essential purchases.

it depends on the job. money is a factor but not the only one. i look at the commute, the team, the tech stack, the work-life balance, and how much i can learn. i also think about where it fits in my long-term career. some things i do to decide:

- make a spreadsheet of the numbers, with the rent, the commute, the income, and how they change over time
- list the pros and cons of each option, like a school essay
- talk to the current team and my own team, to get the real story
- think about the commute and how it changes morning and evening light
- think about how the job changes the routine and if i like the new routine
- think about the people and if i want to be around them every day
- read the company news and see if it's a place i can stay long-term

and then i try to pick one option and commit to it for a while, and not keep second-guessing. the best decision is the one where i wake up the next morning and go "yes, that makes sense" and not "whoops".

Q-01.reply:
ok wait... tbh for me it's all about vibes at first. like an instinctive "yeah this feels right" or "nope something's off." hard to explain but usually i get a read on someone in the first 30 min of meeting them. if that's good, then it's small steps. hangout a few more times, see how they show up and communicate. do they follow through on promises? are they genuinely curious about me or just asking questions to fill silence?

also super important for me is finding shared values and sense of humor - if we're both goofy and lefty and can riff on similar pop culture stuff, that builds rapport fast. but at the end of the day i think trust comes from consistency over time. being reliable, showing up for each other, being honest even when it's hard...

and honestly i'm still figuring this out, especially in a digital age where people can present one way online and be totally different irl. so it's always an ongoing process of refining my radar. 🙃

Q-02.reply:
ugh, this happens like once a month rn. ok wait, first i always listen to them out, even if their concerns don't make sense to me or i feel attacked. they paid for the service after all, so their satisfaction matters.

if it's a legit issue that was my fault (which thankfully isn't often), then i just fix it. no problem, that's what i'm here for. sometimes a small tweak is all it needs, other times we have to go back to square one but whatever, i don't mind putting in the work if it makes them happy.

but if they're just being unreasonable and nitpicking... honestly, tbh, that's when i start reevaluating whether this client is worth my time and energy. i'm not here to be abused or belittled, no matter how much money they might bring in. my self-respect has real value too.

so usually i just calmly explain the scope of work we agreed on and how their new demands go beyond that (if that's the case). if they're still unhappy after that, then maybe it's time to part ways. life's too short to deal with toxic people, even clients.

but like, 9/10 times it gets resolved smoothly. everyone's happy in the end and we can all move on with our lives. 🙃
